title: Monthly count control weakened a one-day excess of distant M6.5+ earthquake pairs in 2001-2024
abstract: We tested whether large earthquakes occurred within one day of each other across distant regions more often than regional time shifts predict. We used 1,093 ComCat events with preferred magnitude at least 6.5 in 2001-2024. Pairs had surface distance above 3,000 km and both events in the same UTC year. Independent shifts within 10-degree cell-years gave 141 observed pairs, a null mean of 115.94, a ratio of 1.216 and an upper-tail Monte Carlo p value of 0.0444. A planned cell-month test gave 140 pairs, a null mean of 124.90, a ratio of 1.121 and p of 0.1409. The M7+ check gave no excess. The primary excess is marginal and depends on the reference model. It does not establish remote triggering or global hazard change. Grid boundaries, retained local clusters, mixed magnitudes, limited counts and assumptions about time shifts limit inference. Code, aggregate counts, all null draws, source hashes, audits and a figure are included. External event records remain outside the baseline package.

display.caption: Distant pair counts under regional time shifts. Blue bars show central 95% null ranges, not effect confidence intervals. The monthly test excludes pairs across month boundaries.

citations.reason: Published annual alignment test motivated a separate within-day test. Source records overlap; this is not independent confirmation.
Reciprocal pair identity informed use of unordered pairs against a shift null instead of a pooled matched-threshold before-after count.
Prior campaign test concerns selected mainshocks and a 500-1500 km ring, a different target.
